processes.description: Staff on the gas and power desks report faults in trading, scheduling and position tools (Sitara, POPS, MIPS, Unify, Enpower, Position Manager, FSP, Tagg, the El Paso scrape) to application or IT contacts, and the reports are often forwarded around the desk. IT announces outages, server migrations and new releases and asks desks to name testers, enter test deals after databases come back, or try new features. Coordinators compile enhancement lists by business unit, and support replies with fixes such as mapping a drive or changing a bridge program.
steps: A user hits a fault (an error on launch, missing curve data, wrong flows or positions) or IT announces an outage, migration or release.
The user reports the symptom and the affected deals or positions to application support or a lead, and the note is forwarded to others on the desk.
Support diagnoses the cause and replies with a fix or workaround, such as mapping a drive or pointing a bridge program at another source.
For enhancements, a coordinator compiles the requested changes by business unit and circulates the list for comment.
Before a release or after maintenance, desks name designated testers, who enter test deals, import schedules or exercise the new feature.
Testers report results back, and outage notices are passed to the desk so work is planned around the downtime.

stalls.summary: Tools fail in day-to-day use: actualization problems in MIPS, errors launching a program or logging on to a server, and a new version missing curve data, each stopping the work until support responds.

Position and volume data come out wrong and have to be reconciled by hand: excessive flow showing in POPS, a short position in Position Manager that is still not working properly weeks later, and TDS position problems.

Planned outages and scrape failures leave systems unavailable for stretches, including weekend maintenance on Enpower, CAPS and the POPS server, Sitara downtime, and an El Paso scrape down through a night shift.
Some failures are local setup problems, such as an unmapped H drive or a missing browser when importing finals, that recur machine by machine until each is fixed.
Follow-through on reported problems is weak: a manager complains of a lack of accountability and no sense of urgency, and a long-demonstrated replacement position manager is still being asked after.

automation.approach: A single issue form or log capturing the system, the exact error text, the affected deals or positions and the desk, with status visible to the requester; a standard post-maintenance and release test checklist (log on, enter and check test deals, import schedules, compare positions); a shared outage calendar fed from IT notices; and a short self-help list of known local fixes such as drive mapping.
automation.rationale: Much of the hands-on work is testing after releases and maintenance and triaging repeat faults. A checklist gives designated testers the same steps each time and lets support clear known local problems quickly, while diagnosing new faults and deciding which enhancements to build stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Many rounds are notices needing little action; others require reproducing an error, checking positions or flows against schedules, entering and verifying test deals after maintenance, or compiling an enhancement list. About 20 minutes covers a typical mix, 60 when a position or flow discrepancy must be reconciled. A checklist and issue form could take over routine testing and triage steps, not diagnosis.

processes.description: Finance coordinators send time-allocation and activity driver surveys for a given month, with a spreadsheet and instructions attached, asking managers to report how their people's time split across activities and commercial teams for the cost and pricing model. Returns are checked against ATEs staffing records, reminders go out on the deadline day, and late responders are chased. Separately, an administrator collects time reports for timekeeping, and staff reply noting vacation, sick or discretionary-holiday days taken.
steps: A finance coordinator sends the survey for the month just ended, attaching the spreadsheet and instructions.
Each manager or employee fills in how their team's time split across activities or commercial teams, sometimes running a supplied file with their own data.
Responses go back to the coordinator, who checks them against ATEs staffing records and queries mismatches.
On the deadline day reminders go out, and late responders are chased afterwards.
The coordinator loads the collected data into the cost or pricing model.
For timekeeping, an administrator asks staff for their time reports and staff reply with any vacation, sick or holiday days taken.

stalls.summary: Survey responses arrive late: a deadline passes with very few completed, deadline-day reminders go out, and surveys for consecutive months end up being requested together.

The same month's data is gathered through parallel requests: separate time and activity surveys sent the same day, and separate requests for model data and pricing data, multiplying the forms each team fills in.
Time reports are collected by asking for them on the due day, with absences reported after the fact in replies.

automation.approach: Prefill each team's survey from ATEs headcount and timekeeping data so respondents only confirm or adjust the split, merge the time and activity surveys into one form per period, send automatic reminders to those who have not returned it before the deadline, and collect absences through a simple form that feeds the time report.
automation.rationale: The work is filling in and compiling the same spreadsheet layout each period and reconciling it with records the company already holds in ATEs. One prefilled combined template removes the duplicate forms and most of the re-keying, while managers still judge how their team's time was really spent.

work_estimate.rationale: Survey rounds need respondents to work out how their team's time split across activities or commercial teams and fill in the spreadsheet, and the coordinator to compile the returns and check them against ATEs before loading the model: about 25 minutes for a typical round, up to 90 when many teams respond or figures are queried. Time-report rounds take a few minutes of noting absences. Prefilling and one combined form could take over much of the compiling.

processes.description: Employees ask their manager for days off or to be put down on the vacation calendar for particular dates. The manager replies granting the request, including short-notice days off, and reminds the person that a longer vacation should be planned in advance the same way as for everyone else in the group. Approved dates are recorded on the group's vacation calendar.
steps: An employee asks the manager for specific days off or to be added to the vacation calendar.
The manager checks the request against the group's coverage and other planned absences.
The manager replies approving the days, or sets the expectation that longer vacations are planned in advance.
The approved dates are entered on the vacation calendar.

automation.approach: A shared vacation calendar with a short request form that shows who else in the group is out on the requested dates, so the manager approves from one view and the approved dates are recorded on the calendar as part of the approval.
automation.rationale: The quotes show brief requests, approvals and entries on the vacation calendar; the work is checking coverage and recording dates, which a shared calendar layout supports. Approval stays a manager's call, as the guidance on planning longer vacations ahead shows.

work_estimate.rationale: Beyond the emails, the hands-on work is checking who else is out on the requested dates and recording the approved days on the vacation calendar: about 3 minutes, up to 10 when dates have to be negotiated against the group's plans. A shared calendar could take over the lookup and recording, not the decision.
